explain.title: The architecture and its parts
explain.body: The Von Neumann architecture is a computer paradigm that delineates a system in which the hardware of the computer has four primary components: the memory, the Central Processing Unit (CPU), input mechanisms, and output mechanisms. Memory holds input data and instructions. Input devices enter data and instructions; output devices present results.

explain.title: The CPU and system bus
explain.body: The CPU has two main components: the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) and the Control Unit (CU). The ALU performs mathematical computations and logical operations. The CU directs tasks and decodes instructions. A system bus is a communication mechanism that facilitates the movement of data between components inside a computational system. Its data bus transports data, address bus maintains data destination information, and control bus transports control electrical signals.

explain.title: The instruction cycle
explain.body: The CPU processes instructions through four steps: fetching, decoding, execution, and storing. The CPU fetches an instruction from memory, the CU decodes it, the CPU executes it, and the result is stored in memory or sent to an output device.

explain.title: Main characteristics and trade-offs
explain.body: Program instructions and data share a single memory store, instructions are processed one after another, and programs are stored in memory and can be changed. This gives simplified design and flexibility. However, the shared memory can cause the Von Neumann bottleneck, and having data and instructions in the same area can create security risks.

mistakes: Leaving out one of the four components: memory, CPU, input devices, and output devices.
Mixing up the ALU and Control Unit: the ALU performs calculations; the CU directs activities and decodes instructions.
Putting the four instruction-cycle steps in the wrong order or replacing the textbook terms with unclear wording.
Saying the bottleneck is simply a slow CPU; it is caused by a single memory area limiting quick retrieval of instructions and data.
Confusing the buses: the data bus transports data, the address bus gives destination information, and the control bus transports control signals.
